explanations.explanation: Bildad does not hold back. He asks Job how long he will go on saying such things, then says, "The words of your mouth are a blustering wind." (Job 8:2) That is Bildad calling Job's whole speech a gust of wind. I think that is a rough way to open.

A dripping roof is a fun picture, but it isn't what Bildad says. He says the words of Job's mouth are "…a blustering wind." (Job 8:2) That is wind, not water. I once had a leaky roof in my own bakery, and nobody called it a speech.
A heavy burden is a real thing to carry, but it isn't Bildad's word. He calls Job's words "…a blustering wind." (Job 8:2) Wind, not weight. The picture he picks is about air.

explanations.answer: He gave them over to their rebellion
explanations.explanation: Bildad says, "When your children sinned against Him, He gave them over to their rebellion." (Job 8:4) That is what Bildad says about Job's children, and it is a hard thing to say to their father. I think this one hurts. Notice that these are Bildad's words, and he is the one making the claim.

explanations.answer: He gave them time to turn back
explanations.explanation: Time to turn back would be a gentler line, but Bildad doesn't say it. He says God "…gave them over to their rebellion." (Job 8:4) Nothing about extra time shows up in his words. It's a heavy moment, so I'll leave it there.

explanations.answer: He sent them away from His presence
explanations.explanation: That one sounds close, but it isn't what Bildad says. His words are that God "…gave them over to their rebellion." (Job 8:4) He doesn't mention being sent away from anywhere. Watch the exact wording, friend, because small swaps change the whole meaning.

Bildad says, "But if you would earnestly seek God and ask the Almighty for mercy…" (Job 8:5) Mercy is what he tells Job to ask for. This is the first of his ifs, and the ifs keep coming. Hold on to this one, because the next verse stacks another on top.
Wisdom is a fine thing to ask for. It just isn't what Bildad says here. His words are, "…ask the Almighty for mercy…" (Job 8:5) Same sentence, different request.

Long life is a nice thing to ask for, but Bildad doesn't bring it up. He says Job should "…ask the Almighty for mercy…" (Job 8:5) That is the request in his if. I'll keep the long life for my birthday wishes.

That's it. Bildad says that if Job is pure and upright, "…even now He will rouse Himself on your behalf and restore your righteous estate." (Job 8:6) Restore means to put back what was there before. Bildad ties it to an if, and that is worth noticing.

Remove would be a gloomy ending, and Bildad is promising the opposite here. He says God "…will rouse Himself on your behalf and restore your righteous estate." (Job 8:6) Restore is the word. Bildad is holding out hope, with a condition attached.

Judge has a stern ring, and Bildad has been stern. But in this verse he says God "…will rouse Himself on your behalf and restore your righteous estate." (Job 8:6) The word is restore. This part of his speech is a promise, as long as Job meets the if.

Bildad says the opposite. He tells Job, "Though your beginnings were modest, your latter days will flourish." (Job 8:7) So the latter days flourish, they don't shrink. Modest beginnings first, then the flourishing.

Right. Bildad says, "Though your beginnings were modest, your latter days will flourish." (Job 8:7) The beginnings are modest and the latter days are the big ones. He is painting a bright picture for Job, with his ifs attached.

explanations.answer: They were born yesterday and know nothing
explanations.explanation: Bildad says, "For we were born yesterday and know nothing; our days on earth are but a shadow." (Job 8:9) He puts himself in with Job when he says "we." It's an odd thing to admit right after a lecture. Still, it's why he points Job to the generations before them.

explanations.answer: They have seen more than their fathers
explanations.explanation: Bildad actually says the reverse. He tells Job to "…consider the discoveries of their fathers." and then says, "…we were born yesterday and know nothing…" (Job 8:8-9) So it's the fathers' discoveries he points to. The "we" are the ones who were born yesterday.

explanations.answer: They are too old to learn anything new
explanations.explanation: Bildad never says anyone is too old. He says, "For we were born yesterday and know nothing; our days on earth are but a shadow." (Job 8:9) That makes them sound young and short on time. Too old is a different complaint, and I'd rather not guess at one.

Yes. Bildad asks, "Will they not teach you and tell you, and speak from their understanding?" (Job 8:10) He is sure the past generations have something to teach Job. He asks it as a question, but I think he already knows the answer he wants.

Bildad says the opposite. He asks, "Will they not teach you and tell you, and speak from their understanding?" (Job 8:10) He expects them to teach Job. The question is how he says it, with a "Will they not…" that sounds pretty sure of itself.

explanations.answer: They dry up faster than grass
explanations.explanation: Bildad says, "While the shoots are still uncut, they dry up more quickly than grass." (Job 8:12) Even uncut, they dry up fast. That is the picture he paints. Grass isn't known for sticking around, so beating it is quite the race.

Locusts are a fair guess, but they aren't in Bildad's picture. He says the shoots "…dry up more quickly than grass." (Job 8:12) The trouble is dryness, not bugs. Nobody in this verse is eating anything.

explanations.answer: They bend low in the wind
explanations.explanation: Bending low in the wind is a good picture, but it isn't Bildad's. He says the uncut shoots "…dry up more quickly than grass." (Job 8:12) Nothing bends here. They just dry out, and fast.
That's right. Bildad says, "Such is the destiny of all who forget God; so the hope of the godless will perish." (Job 8:13) The word he uses is forget. The papyrus and reeds are his picture for that.

Fear is a word you might expect, but it isn't Bildad's word here. He says, "Such is the destiny of all who forget God…" (Job 8:13) The people he is talking about are those who forget. A small word makes a big difference.

Seek is the opposite of where Bildad is headed. He says, "Such is the destiny of all who forget God; so the hope of the godless will perish." (Job 8:13) Seeking was what he told Job to do in verse 5. Forgetting is what he warns about here.
Bildad says, "His confidence is fragile; his security is in a spider’s web." (Job 8:14) That is not much to put your weight on. A spider's web is made to catch bugs, not to hold a person up.

A house on sand is a famous picture, and Jesus uses it in a parable (Matthew 7:26). But Bildad doesn't say it here. He says the man's "…security is in a spider’s web." (Job 8:14) Same idea of shaky ground, different image.
A broken cistern is a picture from another part of the Bible (Jeremiah 2:13), but Bildad doesn't use it. He says, "his security is in a spider’s web." (Job 8:14) Web, not cistern.

Bildad says the opposite. If the plant is uprooted from its place, "…it will disown him, saying, ‘I never saw you.’" (Job 8:18) So the place does not welcome it back. It acts like it never met the plant.
Right. Bildad says that if the plant is uprooted, its place "…will disown him, saying, ‘I never saw you.’" (Job 8:18) I think that is a cold goodbye. The place acts as if it never saw the plant.
Yes. Bildad says, "Surely this is the joy of his way; yet others will spring from the dust." (Job 8:19) So others will spring from the dust. That's what the verse says, and I'll leave the rest alone.

Bildad says it does happen. His words are, "Surely this is the joy of his way; yet others will spring from the dust." (Job 8:19) Others come up from the dust. It sounds like a short bit of news, but it's there in the verse.

That's the word. Bildad says, "Behold, God does not reject the blameless, nor will He strengthen the hand of evildoers." (Job 8:20) It's his big finish, and he sets the blameless and the evildoers side by side.
Test is a word that matters in the book of Job, but it isn't Bildad's word here. He says, "…God does not reject the blameless…" (Job 8:20) The verse is about being rejected or not.

Know is close in feel to some of the talk around here, but it's not in this verse. Bildad says, "…God does not reject the blameless, nor will He strengthen the hand of evildoers." (Job 8:20) Reject is the word he picks.

Bildad says, "He will yet fill your mouth with laughter, and your lips with a shout of joy." (Job 8:21) That's a warm line from a speech that started cold. Laughter is my kind of promise, and I'm glad it's in the passage.

Arguments might fit the way this talk is going, but Bildad doesn't say it. He says God "…will yet fill your mouth with laughter, and your lips with a shout of joy." (Job 8:21) The word is laughter. A shout of joy goes right along with it.

Truth is a good thing to fill a mouth with, but it isn't what Bildad says. He says, "He will yet fill your mouth with laughter, and your lips with a shout of joy." (Job 8:21) The word he uses is laughter, and a shout of joy goes right along with it.
Bildad says the opposite. He says, "Your enemies will be clothed in shame, and the tent of the wicked will be no more." (Job 8:22) Shame is what they wear, not honor. It's a wardrobe nobody wants.
Right. Bildad says, "Your enemies will be clothed in shame, and the tent of the wicked will be no more." (Job 8:22) So it's shame, not honor. That's how he ends his whole speech.
